questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Granting only what a job needs
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to decide which permissions a service account genuinely needs.
questions.stem: Explain how to decide which permissions a service account genuinely needs.

answer.exemplar: Start from what the service actually does, not from what it might need in an emergency. Read the code paths it runs, the tables it touches and the calls it makes, and record each permission those paths need. Then look at what the account currently holds and mark every grant that no current path explains, because permissions are added for one-off reasons and rarely removed afterwards. Those unexplained grants are the candidates for removal, but check for legitimate rare use such as a recovery procedure before cutting. Finally, confirm by running the service with the reduced set, since a permission that looks unnecessary can still be needed on a path that is easy to miss.

questions.explanation: Need is established from observed behaviour, and grants no path explains become removal candidates. Checking rare use and confirming by running the service prevents cutting a needed grant.
questions.hint: Derive need from behaviour, then verify by running it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why layers beat one control
questions.learningObjective: Explain why layered controls reduce risk more reliably.
questions.stem: Explain why layered controls reduce risk more reliably than a single stronger control.

answer.exemplar: A single control has a single point of failure, and the risk of that point is discovered and exploited rather than being averaged away. Layers help because they fail differently: a gateway rule, an application check and a credential design do not share a common cause, so one of them surviving is likely. That also changes the economics of an attacker, who must satisfy several independent conditions instead of one. Layers are not automatically better, and each must genuinely reduce the chance rather than repeat the same check, and the cost has to be weighed against what it buys in a system that is already simple.

questions.explanation: Layers help because they fail independently, so one bypass does not expose the asset. Repeating the same check adds nothing, and each layer carries a cost.
questions.hint: Ask whether each layer fails for a different reason.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Describing a threat actor from behaviour
questions.learningObjective: Write a behavioural actor description that avoids unsupported motive.
questions.stem: Write a behavioural description of a threat actor that avoids unsupported motive.

answer.exemplar: Describe the actor by what was observed rather than by what is assumed. State the observed behaviour precisely: which endpoints were probed, in what sequence, at what times, with what method, and what the party did after each block. Then note the capability the behaviour implies, such as familiarity with the authentication scheme or patience across repeated attempts. Where the evidence is silent, say so rather than filling the gap with a motive, a sponsorship claim or a named group. The point of the description is to help a team decide which behaviour to interrupt, and it does that just as well without the speculation.

questions.explanation: A behavioural description states what was observed and the capability it implies, and marks gaps as gaps. Motive and sponsorship claims are speculation that change no decision.
questions.hint: Describe observations and capability, leave motive out.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Turning a hardening wish into a test
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a hardening wish becomes a testable statement.
questions.stem: Explain how a hardening wish becomes a testable statement.

answer.exemplar: A wish becomes testable when it is rewritten as a condition, an observable and a checker. The wish says we should harden the platform; the testable version says no deployed service may carry a default credential, the state of that setting can be read from the running configuration, and a script asserts it on every build and fails the build when it fails. The transformation is mostly a matter of removing soft language, fixing the subject so it is unambiguous, and naming what will look at it and how often. Softened wording such as where practical, and a review by the team, are the usual signs that a requirement has not been made testable yet.

questions.explanation: A testable statement names a condition, an observable and a checker, with no soft qualifiers. Wishes that survive in reviews and plans have not been reduced to something a script can fail.
questions.hint: Remove the soft words, then name the checker.

questions.topic: A service outside the inventory
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an undeclared service is a structural risk.
questions.stem: Explain why an undeclared service is a structural risk rather than a paperwork gap.

answer.exemplar: An undeclared service is structural because everything the organisation does about protection is driven by what it believes it owns. If a service is missing from the architecture then no owner reviews its patches, no hardening baseline is applied to it, no monitoring watches it and no change record describes it. Its data may still flow through pipelines that are otherwise well controlled, so sensitive information crosses a component that nobody hardened. Paperwork would fix the diagram; the structural risk is that the control set has a hole in it, and that hole stays open until the service is discovered, adopted, and given the same treatment as everything else.

questions.explanation: Protection follows what the organisation believes it owns, so an undeclared service sits outside patching, hardening and monitoring. Fixing the diagram alone leaves the hole in the control set open.
questions.hint: Ask what it does to services it believes it owns.

questions.topic: Describing a threat actor from behaviour
questions.learningObjective: Select the actor description that the evidence supports.

stimulus.body: A behaviour log records a party enumerating tenants over four nights, collecting no data, and abandoning the attempt after each account was locked. The log notes no credential reuse and no privilege escalation anywhere in the attempts.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Requiring two people for one action
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a two-person rule changes the effect of an error.
questions.stem: Explain why a two-person rule changes what a single person's error can cause.

answer.exemplar: A single approver can carry one mistake all the way through, because there is no second reading of the change before it lands in production. The second approver introduces a check that is independent of the person who wrote the change, so the same error has to survive two readings rather than one, and the common cases, a typo in a resource name, a destructive default, a missing condition, get caught. The rule does not make errors impossible and it does not protect against two people sharing the same wrong assumption or an attacker who can supply two identities. It reduces the chance that one person's oversight becomes production, which is why it belongs on rare and hard to reverse actions rather than on routine ones.

questions.explanation: A second independent reading means a single mistake must survive twice, so common errors are caught before they land. It does not protect against shared assumptions or two compromised identities.
questions.hint: Ask how many independent readings an error must survive.

answer.exemplar: For a service account, least privilege means the account can reach only what the service genuinely uses, so that a stolen credential or a hijacked dependency buys an attacker a narrow path rather than the whole platform. It does not stop the credential from being stolen, it does not protect the actions the account is genuinely allowed to take, and it does not cover a design in which one service legitimately needs broad access to everything. It also does not remove the value of a second control, since a narrow scope and an independent check answer different questions. answer.exemplar: Write the role from the work outward rather than from the platform inward. questions.topic: Why layers beat one control
questions.learningObjective: Explain how layering changes the meaning of a bypass.
questions.stem: Explain how layered controls change the meaning of a bypass.

answer.exemplar: With a single control, a bypass is effectively the end of the story, because the asset behind it is now exposed and everything else the platform does happens afterwards. With layers, a bypass is one failed condition rather than an outcome, and the meaning of the same event changes: it tells you something about that layer rather than about the whole system. This is what makes layered designs worth their cost, because the failure stays bounded and the evidence about what went wrong survives. The benefit only holds if the layers are independent, so if they share a cause then a single bypass takes them all and the meaning is exactly the same as it would have been without layering at all.

questions.explanation: With layers a bypass becomes one failed condition that stays bounded and still tells you something useful, if the layers fail for different reasons. Shared causes restore the single point of failure.
questions.hint: Ask whether one failure removes every layer.

answer.exemplar: Describe the party from the record outwards. questions.topic: Why layers beat one control
questions.learningObjective: Compute the attempts that reach the end after several layers.
questions.stem: A design uses 4 layers and each layer blocks half of the attempts that reach it. How many attempts out of 100 reach the end?
questions.explanation: Four halvings take 100 to 50, then 25, then 12.5, then 6.25. The compounding shows why the remainder matters: an attempt has to satisfy every layer, and each failure point is a place to intervene.
questions.hint: Halve the count once for each of the four layers.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Granting only what a job needs
questions.learningObjective: Compute the value produced by a worked example.

stimulus.body: A worked example in the architecture guide shows a worker role that reads one table and writes to one queue. The role currently holds 7 permissions, and the guide records that the proposed change removes 3 of them.

questions.stem: Using the worked example, what value does the calculation produce?

options.text: The role holds 21 permissions afterwards, because each permission counts three times in the role definition.
options.misconception: multiplies the grant count by an invented factor

options.text: The role holds 10 permissions afterwards, because the change adds the removed grants back in another form.
options.misconception: invents extra grants for the same work

options.text: The role holds 7 permissions afterwards, because removing grants never changes the total.
options.misconception: claims removals do not affect the count

options.text: The role holds 4 permissions afterwards, because 7 minus 3 leaves that figure.

questions.explanation: Seven permissions minus the three removed leaves 4 on the role, which is the figure the change produces. Adding grants back or multiplying by an invented factor contradicts the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Subtract the removed grants from the starting total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What least privilege does and does not do
questions.learningObjective: Decide which grants to remove and count the excess left behind.
questions.stem: Decide which grants to remove, then count the excess permissions left behind.

options.text: Remove nothing, because the excess is small enough that the review is not worth the disruption.
options.misconception: dismisses a small excess as not worth acting on

options.text: Remove every grant above four permissions, so 6 excess permissions remain and the small roles are untouched.
options.misconception: uses a fixed threshold instead of the task evidence

options.text: Remove the grants no task explains, so 5 excess permissions remain across the four roles.
Remove all grants from the two largest roles, so 12 excess permissions remain and the rest are untouched.
options.misconception: clears whole roles instead of excess grants

questions.explanation: Removing grants that no described task explains leaves 5 excess permissions across the four roles. A fixed threshold, or clearing entire roles, removes or retains the wrong things.
questions.hint: Remove only what the tasks cannot explain.
